That is the situation as I
see it. One does not want to be sentimental about the matter; but one wants to see the facts as they are. The situation should be remedied and if it be of any avail I should like to add my voice to that of the hon. member for South Wellington who yesterday left the door open to the government to do what, not only from a humanitarian standpoint, but even from the lower ground of policy, is one of the best things they could do.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MH. HEAPS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding all that has been said to the contrary I believe the unemployment question to-day is a national one. The Dominion is practically in control of all policies relating to labour, for instance, immigration, et cetera. That unemployment will occur during the winter months is perhaps inevitable because of our climate, but for the whole of 1929 work was scarce for all those who seek their living by their day's wage. In any case, unemployment is not an emergent question to-day; it is with us and with us to stay. The question is whether we want to tackle the problem in the manner we should. Unemployment insurance, while

Unemployment-Mr. Evans
not a cure, will at least relieve the sufferings of many, some of which sufferings I myself saw last winter.
There are many causes for unemployment and I am going to enumerate some of them. One fact that we must face in our economic life to-day is that we are everlastingly driving our workers into our industrial centres, our cities. Our population is being more and more separated into two distinct groups; and we need not seek very far for the cause. In the cities we have the capitalists and the wage earners; in the country we are getting more and more into the way of the older countries, and we have the landlord and the tenant; both these groups corresponding to the old days of feudal lord and serf.
The high cost of living certainly debars many people from entering into small industries and concerns for themselves; it puts all such enterprises out of reach of those who are willing to work. I meet to-day in the country many who express their desire to go into poultry raising or dairying on a small scale, believing that the family could keep those things going while it was profitable for the father to work out while wages were at their highest. But it seems to me that the policy which our friends to my right are advocating is killing this spirit of enterprise, and we are driving our population into two distinct groups.
Let us see what the man who would go into an industry on a small scale is up against. First he builds a house, however humble it may be. He goes to the lumber yard nearest to him and there he finds that the price of common lumber, probably planed on one side and one edge, is as high as $56 a thousand retail in any yard in Saskatchewan to-day. Perhaps he asks the price of siding and finds it runs all the way from $80 to $90 a thousand, I believe a good deal dearer than the price at which the mills in British Columbia have been delivering it in the Orient. He can, however, secure at $62 a thousand a grade of siding which, I would draw to the attention of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), carries a 25 per cent duty. This is the cheapest grade of siding at present in the yards in the west. It is called No. 2^ siding, and it is cut, I believe, from stumps, such as fallen logs that are over ripe. He can get this for $62 a thousand by calling a five-and-a-half-inch board six inches. Sometimes it is five and three-eighths inches, but he must pay for six inches. Every worker, too, must buy flour, and he finds that a sack of good household flour costs about eighty
cents more to-day at his point than the price at which the same grade made from Canadian wheat is quoted in Liverpool. In fact, flour, Manitoba Top Patents, is sold at about $1.69 per barrel cheaper in Liverpool than in Winnipeg. If he goes into dairying he finds himself up against a fiscal policy which can easily be explained by the action of the government in removing all protection on the dairy products which he expects to produce and placing it on the necessaries of life which he must buy, tending still further to herd our workers into the cities. Let me give a case in point. To provide that freer entry into the Australian market for the manufacture of Canada the government took three cents a pound duty off butter and placed it on raisins. In fact, this was the foundation of the Australian treaty. I would not mention it but for the fact that it seems to have been the policy of governments in this country for the last sixty years so to divide our people into two distinct groups, the capitalists and the wage earners. When there was a duty on butter which promised to be a factor in price fixing, it was at once taken off and that duty was placed on the necessaries of life. The old duty on butter was four cents a pound, but it was never then of any use to the farmer.
The efficiency of any nation must always be judged according to the cost of living and the cost of production in that country, and not by the ease with which the earnings of the worker are filched from him, which in the past has been mistakenly called prosperity. Land is cheap all over Canada to-day. It is the necessaries for settlement that are beyond the reach of the worker's energy and enterprise. We guarantee the profits of the owners of urban industry, but there is absolutely no security for the workingman, particularly the unskilled. There is no security either for the man on the farm. Everything seemingly is done to aid the capitalists, whose profits are guaranteed; but the workers are herded together without any consideration for their well-being. Urban industry to-day seems nothing better than an excuse to secure privileges by legislation and to filch the earnings of the farmer and the worker.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said that capital was the great essential in industry. The great essential in industry, to my way of thinking, is energy and enterprise, and the end in view should always be the well-being of the subject. I had a resolution sent in to me, which I passed on to the Prime

Unemployment-Mr. Evans
Minister, from the Biggar division of the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway Employees, and it reads this way:
Whereas it has been brought to our attention that thousands of railway employees who would normally have steady employment throughout the year have been laid off, and are feeling severe privation 'and hardship resulting therefrom,
Be it therefore resolved that Biggar division No. 151, Canadian Brotherhood of Railway Employees, go on record as favouring a conference of representatives of the financial, industrial and labour organizations being called with a view to stimulating industry, restoring the confidence of the public, and reducing unemployment.
The Minister of Labour says that the Dominion government has no responsibility in the matter of calling a conference to consider the question of unemployment. I have thought since that perhaps it was a good thing that a conference was not called on the spur of the moment, because after calm and more mature consideration a commission may be appointed, composed of men of economic thought and foresight, who will go to the root of the matter and find some permanent solution of the problem for the future as well as the present. The fact is that the worker's lot in Canada-and I must say that it is also the lot of the farmer, who is being continually driven into the industrial centres-is a precarious and haphazard one, subject to all kinds of class legislation and class privileges which neither the agriculturist nor the workingman shares. The ease with which production is carried on should be a national benefit. If it is easier to produce, it should be easier for the workingman as well as the capitalist. To the capitalist, ease of production is a bonanza; but to the wage earner it is a nightmare.
I was struck by a remark of the hon. member for Toronto-Scarborough (Mr. Harris) in his speech the other day. He wants the farmer to make more butter, and he would place a duty on butter for that purpose. He really is speaking there for the great creamery combine or merger which is being formed to control that business from one end of this Dominion to the other, and for which he wants to secure all kinds of advantages. When the farmer's wife was the butter maker, everything she needed was, in price, out of line with the butter which she made and sold. But now that the merger is being formed, every advantage will be given to it, particularly the power of price fixing.
As I said before, the farmer has to pay high duties. He is penalized on all his raw material. Take salt, for instance. The packers and fish curers can get their salt in free, but the farmer must pay a high duty,

not only on the salt itself, but on the covers containing the salt. By these means the small farmer is soon driven to throw up his hands and to tell the mortgage holder or the banker to take what is left, and he himself then crowds in with those who are already standing outside the factory doors in our industrial centres waiting for employment.
The hon. member for Toronto-Scarborough, who made a very good speech in a way, deplored the fact that we were importing a large quantity of foodstuffs which we might be producing here. Yet he very illogically advocates an increase in tariffs, which is the very bane of agriculture. He never told us, though, with what we pay for the goods we import. If the price of farm products today were in line with the price of manufactured goods, and the farmer were given, the freedom of exchange which he needs, there would be a rush to the farm, and more people would be making their own living. Intensive farming would be the result, and our cities would not, even in the wintertime, be overburdened with workers. The means of production here should be the cheapest in the world. They say that unemployment exists in England as well as in Canada-one a free trade and the other a protectionist country; but the difference lies in this, that in England land is very dear, here it is cheap. In fact one of my protectionist friends told me not so long ago that if a farmer wants to sell out to-day in Ontario all he expects to get for his farm is the cost of his buildings -very little more. Indeed, I know one farmer who did sell out for less than the buildings could be put up to-day. That means the land is within reach of everybody, but the necessaries to make it productive are out of reach of the man who in an honest and humble way, with his own courage and enterprise, can make it go. Here is one of the real causes of unemployment at the present time.
Now, the demand for unemployment insurance is simply a natural growth of urban industry, as our fiscal policy is maintained to-day. We are subject to panics and industrial depression, very often seemingly for no cause whatever. The present situation may have been brought about largely through a bearish pressure on the stock market, which created a lack of confidence, and that in turn brought about a period of under-consumption. This is a fact anyway, that underconsumption is not only rife amongst the working class who are out of work, but people of independent means have curtailed purchases to bare necessities. The curtailing of the British preference by the latest restriction, a

Unemployment-Mr. Evans
measure brought into force by our government a year ago, has prevented, I feel, a very large portion of our wheat being moved, and in this way we have the cause of unemployment accounted for in large measure.
It is a terrible indictment of our economic system that while our warehouses are full of manufactured goods and our granaries are full of grain, our industrial centres are full of hungry people out of work. Our manufacturers for whom this nation has been bled white take upon themselves no responsibility for the welfare of the men and women who work in their factories, and on the most flimsy excuses they have thrown them out of employment. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company, which was actively engaged in immigration, turned immigrants loose on a sympathetic rural municipality or village without any further care for them. I have here a letter written by the pastor of one of the churches in MacGregor, Manitoba, in which he says:
I had made up my mind to write you regarding a number of Welsh miner immigrants. Their statement to me was that they had come to Canada under what was known as the Canadian Pacific Railway cottage scheme. Their passage was paid, and then when they arrived in Canada they were to be put in a cottage with furniture supplied, and at once they were to receive wages amounting to about five dollars per day. Then after a year's experience on a farm they were to be placed in charge of a farm for themselves, etc. Rosy and bright was it not? When they arrived here, the cottages were old, unused, unfurnished houses, and there were no farmers looking for men at any such wages. I do not think much is to be gained by having men come to Canada under any such conditions, but at the same time the citizens of Canada ought not to permit any company whatsoever to bring immigrants here and dump them on a community in the expectation that the neighbours of those unfortunates would not see them starve. Four of the five families went into Winnipeg securing work for the summer, but how about the winter ?
They are there to-day, swelling the ranks of the unemployed.
Regarding the conference which the Minister of Labour has been urged to call, the Saskatoon Star has this to say:	'
Only the Dominion government can take a proper survey of the economic problems thus created, chiefly the problem of seasonal unemployment. This is very clearly a national issue. No province or municipality can see the whole of it or attempt to control the movement of seasonal workers.
There are other reasons why the Dominion government has a duty to give a lead. It is responsible for immigration policy. It can, if it chooses, shut the door tight on immigration or open it wide and the policy it elects to follow evidently has an important bearing on the state of the labour market. Again, the
Dominion government is the only government in the country which has any control over the monetary and financial policies of the banks, another powerful factor in limiting or enlarging opportunities for employment.
I think a duty rests there on the Dominion government, and I shall hope to see a commission appointed that will go to the root of this matter. A similar resolution to the one I have already read was passed by the United Farmers of Canada at a conference composed of the executive of the united farmers, the trades and labour council and the churches in Saskatoon. They, too, called on the government to investigate the present situation. I believe with the Star that the government must take the responsibility in a very large measure for unemployment, seeing that they control practically all the policies relating to labour conditions. I believe, too, that the present crisis is largely due to the inelasticity of credit. In point of fact, since the bank is the nerve centre of modern business, all crises are financial more or less.
Now, whatever we do, there is a duty we owe to those who are suffering hunger and the want of the necessaries of life, and without doubt some way will have to be found to bring about a scheme of unemployment insurance. The responsibility for this must be placed on the protected industries, and I believe with a proper system of such insurance based on the responsibility of the protected parties, the manufacturers of this country, a far more stable condition of affairs would be brought about. I am sure that under such a scheme employers could not create panics in the hearts of their workers through the threat of taking their jobs to the extent that it is done to-day. Labour is itinerant because of the uncertainty of employment. Employment insurance must be based chiefly on protected industry. Established industry in Canada to-day has an assurance which is not enjoyed by capitalists in any other country, and these capitalists must be made responsible for the working men whom they have induced to take employment in their factories. At the conference held by the United Farmers of Saskatchewan, the secretary of the trades and labour council told us that a very large concern which had established itself in Regina employed last year about a thousand workers. It laid off practically three-quarters of them at the beginning of this winter. When the manager was consulted he made the statement that it was the policy of his company to have one man on the job and two at the gate. It is unreasonable to expect that the nation's workers should be subjected to the exigencies of capitalism, and panics created to satisfy

Unemployment-Mr. Evans
greed. I would tolerate protection in some form, and to some extent, if it were extended to the worker, but it is unreasonable to tax their necessaries of life. If the protectionist system, which at the present time is only a debauch, could be extended to the worker, and give some assurance to the wage earner, it might be more tolerable. There is no stability in our present method of manufacturing and distributing goods, and we may as well ask ourselves what it is that gives value to the subscribed capital of going concerns, all of which depend upon the exploitation of the people. It depends very largely on the control of parliament by the capitalistic concerns of to-day. Let me quote the words of Roger Babson, that great wizard of business and finance. This is what he has to say in regard to capitalistic investments:
The value of our investments depends not on the strength of our banks but rather on the strength of our churches. The underpaid preachers of the nation are the men upon whom we are really depending, rather than the well paid lawyers, bankers and brokers. The religion of the community is really the bulwark of our investments.
To my mind those words are rather significant. It is a telling indictment against our present business methods when it can be said that the safety of the whole structure depends, not on a square deal for all, but on the want of proper information and the piety of our people.
Of the country's earnings last year, the banks took some $27,915,255 in net profits. Exorbitant profits mean under-consumption. We only need to know something of the A.B.C. of economics to understand that the fact that there are exorbitant profits means that there must be under-consumption. I have the following figures as to the net profits of Canadian banks, obtained from the bureau of statistics:
Bank of Montreal	 $7,070,892
Bank of Toronto	 1,453,436
Banque Provinciale du Canada.	551,622
Canadian Bank of Commerce..	5,066,229
Royal Bank of Canada	 7,145,137
Imperial Bank of Canada.. ..	1,561,561
Banque Canadienne Nationale.	1,053,099
The profits of the Bank of Nova Scotia, the Dominion bank and the Weyburn Security bank are not given. If we take the returns of those three as published last year and add them to the others, it brings the total amount up to about $30,000,000. This is so much money taken out of the Canadian industry. Canadian industry during 1930 will be that much more dependent upon borrowed money, unless agriculture is able to export at a profit what it has on hand. We have been able

to meet these exorbitant profits by expanding agriculture year by year, but agriculture has reached the stage where it can no longer bear the strain. I see no hope of equity between the classes so long as our present system of privilege continues, and exorbitant profits are taken each year from the earnings of the workers. In fact, to me it is no wonder there is unemployment; big profits, I say, cause under-consumption. Credit and banking should be public utilities, publicly owned and controlled. More and more it becomes evident that the state must assume certain functions hitherto not deemed to be appropriate to it. Canada's inefficiency to-day is to be seen in the cost of living and the cost of production. The cost of living in Canada is higher than in any country to which she exports her goods, whether they be agricultural products or manufactured articles. Such a condition cannot be very long continued; the cost of living and the cost of production must be lowered as the first step in solving the unemployment problem.
With regard to the Prime Minister's speech yesterday, I want to say that if this government refuses to cooperate with the provinces, then the provinces, as sovereign entities, will have to take steps to protect themselves. In the past neither the Dominion nor the provincial governments have had any control over the welfare of our people, as a result of whose brawn and sweat the industries of this country have been established. The fiscal policy of this country has been in the hands of the capitalists, who nominally own the industrial plants of the Dominion. I say they only nominally own the plants which they direct, and with which they exploit the workers of the country. Neither Roger Babson's method, the capitalistic control of parliament, nor .even the militia will be able to hold this country in peace, order and good government if the railway companies and other concerns, such as Besco, are allowed to import labour, as they import raw material, for their own .benefit. I have here a clipping from the Toronto Star which describes conditions in the United States and contains also a warning which was thrown out the other day to one of the committees of congress in Washington. The clipping is dated April 1, 1930, and states:
The country is faced with possibility of revolution unless the unemployment situation is met, William Green of the American Federation of Labour warned the Senate Commerce Committee to-day demanding enactment of the three pending Wagner bills to alleviate conditions.

Unemployment-Mr. Ryerson
Conditions are much the same in this country; we are following exactly the same policy that has brought United States agriculturists to the point where they must accept direct aid.

I am in sympathy with the purpose of this bill, but I am afraid, Mr. Speaker, that clause 4 makes it a money bill, and therefore out of order. Apart from that, the bill does conflict in some degree with the working of the Workmen's Compensation Act of the province of Quebec. The Workmen's Compensation Act of that province is different from any other provincial act so far as I am aware, inasmuch as under the Quebec act employers are required to insure their employees with some insurance company. Employers are permitted to insure in any company they choose, subject to the approval of the Workmen's Compensation Board of the province. So that the Quebec Act, and the commission appointed under that act, have full control over the insurance under which the workmen are insured. Of course, the age of the workmen is a big factor in determining the premium that is to be paid by the employer, and I suppose that many employers of labour in the province are taking advantage of that fact and insuring their employees up to a certain age limit. That operates in the way my hon. friend has indicated, so that there is an age beyond which an employer does not insure his men and still have them protected under the Workmen's Compensation Act.
I am not sure whether my hon. friend from St. Ann (Mr. Guerin) knows that the labour representatives have been encouraged to expect that at the next session of the legislature of the province of Quebec the provincial act will be amended to place it on a somewhat similar basis to that of the Ontario act, which



Unemployment-Mr. Ryerson
provides for state insurance rather than insurance by a company.
Apart from the fact that this is a money bill, I have only this to add. There is a principle in this bill which we might consider, and I think it might well be considered under Bill No. 149, which is now before the house. I feel that we might be able to provide by regulation that workmen shall not be debarred from employment on public works simply because of their age. If my hon. friend will withdraw the measure I will undertake to see if we can incorporate such a provision in our own regulations.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT CONTRACTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I cannot see that there is any proposal in my bill to spend money, unless it be in the last clause referring to the fair wage that should be paid. I am quite willing to withdraw the clause, as I believe it will be covered by the regulations that are being prepared by the Minister of Labour; but I am not inclined to withdraw the three other clauses unless I see similar provisions written into the minister's bill. I do not know how far it would be in order for me to ask you to allow my bill to stand until I have an opportunity of seeing the clauses to be incorporated in the minister's bill, but if they do not cover what I am trying to provide for in my bill I shall be obliged to ask the house to proceed with it. I do not say that by way of a threat; I want to be as respectful as possible to the minister.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HE.APS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I had nearly finished describing the sad experience of a number of British families who were brought to this country last summer. It is not my intention to set out in detail the disappointments and sufferings of these people. But is it any wonder they should strongly resent their treatment? I submit, sir, that the whole shameful proceedings constitute a blot upon the fair name of Canada-a blot which should be wiped out at the earliest opportunity. I do not blame the government for the manner in which these people have been deceived, or for the treatment handed out to them upon their arrival here, but I do desire to point out that in permitting and assisting in this kind of immigration the government is imposing additional burdens upon the municipalities affected, and for that reason is morally bound to assume some responsibility.
Another point which I should like to bring to the attention of the house is this: that while there are unemployment problems and trade depression throughout the world, these conditions in Canada are, in my opinion, caused by the policies of this government in tinkering with the tariff and in lowering the tariff protection in certain lines of industries, which has made possible importation of enormous quantities of products of all kinds, any considerable portion of which, if produced or manufactured here, would have furnished employment for the greater part of those who to-day are unemployed. In that respect may I point out as one example the importation of agricultural implements for the calendar year 1929. The figures furnished by the bureau of statistics show for the period named that we imported agricultural implements to the startling amount of $31,845,326. Had one-half of these implements been manufactured in Canadian plants, we would have no unemployment in my constituency. This is only one example; there are many others of a similar nature affecting different centres of industry.
Before concluding my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I desire to call the attention of the house to an incorrect statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in the course

Unemployment-Mr. Campbell
of his speech yesterday which I am sure he will desire to have corrected. He stated that unemployment was of a local nature in certain provinces only, and for the province of Ontario, Port Arthur, Kenora and Toronto were the only centres mentioned. In making this statement he evidently overlooked a large deputation representing many Ontario municipalities which waited upon the hon. the Minister of Labour on February 3rd in respect to this matter. In confirmation of this I desire to quote the Brantford Expositor of February 4, 1930:
Mayor Beckett Is Disappointed Sees Little Hope of Getting Federal Unemployment Assistance Says Critical Time is Now, Not Six Weeks Hence
Mayor Beckett who returned with Alderman Linscott from Ottawa where they were members of the deputation waiting upon the government yesterday with regard to unemployment matters, expressed himself this morning as disappointed with the prospects of getting assistance. 'The mayor was one of five spokesmen chosen for a very large deputation from many Ontario municipalities. He stressed the fact that the critical time in unemployment was right now and assistance not forthcoming before a month or six weeks' time would be too late to meet the real needs. He discussed the unemployment conditions in Brantford at this time and told the Minister of Labour, Hon. Peter Heenan, that with the assurance of Premier Ferguson that Ontario would bear a one-third share of the excess cost of local improvement works undertaken during the winter as relief measures, an assurance that the federal government would bear a like proportion, would enable him to telegraph a message at once to Brantford that would enable the Brantford city council, in session last night, to provide for an immediate start on an extensive program of local improvement work. Without the minister's assurance the much needed work could not be undertaken as under the act the city and the taxpayer on whose frontage the local improvements were constructed must bear the cost in certain proportions. Under the present winter conditions the cost of such work was three times what it would be under summer conditions. The property owners and taxpayers could not in fairness be asked to bear this extra burden, and the assistance from the provincial government was conditional upon a corresponding contribution from the Dominion government.
I will not read the whole report, but will merely give the last paragraph:
Expressing his disappointment this morning, Mayor Beckett commented that "When you have got to carry politics to the length to forget about the actual needs of the citizens in the communities, it is time we got rid of politics." The need for assistance he said, was immediate, and from the result of the meeting with the minister it appeared "just a case of these politicians passing the buck, one to another." 2419-82J
I hold in my hand a series of resolutions from the Brantford Unemployment Association which I would like to present to the house. This resolution is dated March 12, 1930, and is as follows:
Whereas the unemployed in Brantford have found it necessary to organize an association for their own protection and whereas unemployment is the natural result of the application of power and labour saving machinery to industry,
And whereas this association is of the opinion that a system of unemployment insurance is the only logical solution of the problem of unemployment,
Therefore be it resolved that this Brantford Unemployment Association petition the federal and provincial governments to take immediate steps to enact legislation providing for a system of unemployment insurance, and be it further resolved that in the opinion of this association the provincial and federal governments should immediately take such steps as may be necessary to permit of the federal government assuming full responsibility for the relief of unemployment in all parts of the Dominion.
This resolution is signed by James Robson Humble, 68 Queen Street, Brantford, Ontario.

good deal of the discussion on the question of unemployment has hinged around the question of the relative responsibilities of the federal government and the various provincial governments. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) admits that the problem of unemployment is national in character, but he does not admit federal responsibility. It seemed to me that in his speech the Prime Minister attempted to put some of us who are supporting this resolution in a false position before the public by deploring the advertising that the debate gives to adverse conditions in the country. I cannot agree with such a proposition. As some other speaker said this afternoon, that is simpl.v the attitude of the ostrich; he sticks his head in the sand and persuades himself that the problem does not exist. It seems to me that the only sane way to deal with problems of this nature is to face them; we must admit that they exist and do what we reasonably can to meet the situation. May I in this connection quote the late President Wilson:
That man is not a pessimist who, when he sees the funnel shaped cloud approaching directs the feet of his wife and children towards the cyclone cellar; but the man is not an optimist, he is a fool-nay, a criminal-who at that critical moment neglects his parental duty and stands agape rejoicing in the manifestations of nature.
It seems to me this quotation has an application in the problem we have before us.

Unemployment-Mr. Campbell
I was surprised to hear the Prime Minister say that no representations had been made to him on the question of unemployment by the various provincial governments. At the recent conference held in the east block representations were made by three prairie governments, those of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HE.APS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am glad to accept
the word of the Prime Minister, and am pleased that he has set the matter right. Naturally I was very much disturbed, the same as many other hon. members, to hear the Prime Minister say that no relief would be given to the province of Saskatchewan because there is a government other than Liberal in that province. The Prime Minister did admit, rather grudgingly I think, that he was prepared to give some assistance to Progressive governments, but none at all to other provincial governments. In other words, in order for the poor, needy people to get consideration from the federal government they must obey the dictum to elect nothing but straight Liberal governments. I wonder if the Prime Minister would treat his own constituency of Prince Albert in a similar fashion. That is the constituency from whence he derived his seat in parliament; I wonder if he will tell the needy and hungry people there that they cannot secure consideration in this parliament because of the fact that the people in Saskatchewan have a government other than Liberal.
I enjoyed, as I am sure other members did, ihe extracts that the Prime Minister was pleased to read from his book entitled Industry and Humanity. I agree with all the statements he read. I always like to think of the Prime Minister as the man who wrote Industry and Humanity; I like to think of him as a humanitarian, and a man whose heart and sympathy go out to the common people. But, Sir, when I place the quotations from that book along with the statement he made in the house, I wonder what to make of it.
(Mr. Campbell.]
I agree with the quotations from the book; I agree with everything that the book contains, and it was a shock to hear the Prime Minister couple with his quotations the statement that relief would be withheld from those provinces who were represented by other than Liberal governments. When one compares that statement with the idealism, the altruism and noble sentiments expressed in the book, one begins to wonder if in the physical form of the Prime Minister there are two opposing spirits; one wonders, to use a common literary expression, whether he represents both Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde. However, I am inclined to agree with the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine)-as a matter of fact, I think we all do-that the exactions and nervous strain imposed upon one holding so high and responsible a position as the Prime Minister must be very severe, and it is possible that when the Prime Minister made that statement, he was not in his normal temper or his normal state of mind. I can scarcely think that he was.
It is regrettable that this question of unemployment, involving the welfare and happiness of thousands of women and children, should be considered in the party spirit we have witnessed in this debate. It is my opinion that the question cannot properly be considered in this partisan atmosphere. It is something which calls for the cool deliberation of scientists and economists; it is not for the consideration of politicians who are placed in a political atmosphere.
When we come to the question of the relative responsibilities of provincial and federal governments I certainly cannot agree with the Prime Minister or with those who claim that this is a purely provincial or municipal matter. Let us take the case of a municipality that deals effectively with the problem, looks after its unemployed and provides relief or work, and compare it with the municipality which does not care for its unemployed. What is the logical outcome? The needy who are looking for work come into the municipality where work is being provided and where the people are being looked after. I can see no way in which to avoid such a situation. As a matter of fact, how can we prevent the needy, those who are out of work, from spreading from one province to another? To my mind there is only one government that can stop the people coming into the country, and that is the federal government which has control of immigration. For these reasons I say there is no way in which one municipality or one province can deal effectively with this problem. I am not one

Unemployment-Mr. Campbell
of those people who would lay the whole responsibility at the feet of this government- certainly not. There are great economic forces at work in the world to-day which neither this government nor any other government can control. We have to recognize that. These are world conditions, and Canada is only a small unit.
To come down to the local consideration of the question, however, and to deal with it as it affects Canada and as perhaps we might be able to control it, I would put the problem under three heads. I would say that first the trouble was caused by the recent stock market crash and the consequent reduction of the purchasing power of hundreds of thousands of people. That has had wide ramifications in industry and in finance, and naturally it has had a great deal to do with the unemployment conditions which exist today. Then I would say the reduction in wheat prices has had some effect, and of course that also is to some extent a reaction from the stock market crash and the consequent curtailment of buying by farmers. Under the third head I would put the large immigration into Canada during the past few years. There is no question about federal responsibility for immigration. During the last three years we took in 330,000 immigrants. The Prime Minister referred to complaints made against the government because immigration into this country was not large enough. Probably that may have been so, but I can inform him that no such complaint ever came from this section of the house. From 1922 up to the present time the group in this section of the house has protested against a vigorous immigration policy. We never took the stand that people should not be allowed into the country, but we were opposed to the activities either of the government or of transportation companies in order to induce people to come here.
May I say in connection with the number of immigrants brought in during the past year, which amounted to 165,000, that never at any time in the history of the United States was that country ever called upon to absorb so large a percentage of its own population as Canada was during last year, and ordinarily that would not be considered a very large number of immigrants to come to this country. I think the immigration into the country during the past few years has had something to do with the increase in wheat acreage, and of course that has had an effect on prices.
Then there is another question, and this of course is related to the question of the stock market. It involves the whole money system, and the question arises as to whether or not
we have the right money system. The matter of inflation and deflation has a great deal to do with unemployment, with business stagnation and with distress both in the rural and urban sections of the country. The hon. member for Westaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) last night gave it as his opinion that the unemployment in England to-day was the direct result of the deflation policy adopted by the British banks in 1920. Canada adopted the same policy, as did the United States. However, we are much younger countries, with greater resources, and it did not affect us so badly as it affected Great Britain. With that assertion I agree, and I think the reason that France has been in the happier position of recent years of having no unemployment problem is due in a very large measure at any rate to the fact that she did not permit deflation.
The hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer) this afternoon dealt with the question of the gold standard. The question as to whether or not getting away from the gold standard would change this condition is a very large matter. I have under my hand an article commenting on a book written by Professor Irving Fisher of Yale. In this book Professor Fisher points out that the trouble with the gold standard is that the unit of value, the measurement of value, is changing all the time. He has one remedy for dealing with the question, and the article points out that another remedy, from a different angle but involving the same thing, is put forward by Maynard Keynes, the distinguished economist of Great Britain. There is no doubt that the changing of the unit of value had a great deal to do with these problems.
Let me illustrate it in this way. We will say that a farmer secures 1,000 bushels of oats from a neighbour. The unit of measurement is a bushel, which is 34 pounds. If that unit is changing all the time, the way the dollar is changing in value, what is the result? The farmer incurs a liability for 1,000 bushels of oats, to be paid back perhaps in a year's time, but if at the end of the year, when his liability becomes due, he finds that he must pay back 1,000 bushels of oats on the basis of 60 pounds to the bushel, his debt is nearly doubled. That is the situation of thousands of farmers, business men and manufacturers to-day. Those who incurred liabilities even a year ago; those who borrowed money or incurred any kind of liability and are forced to-day, under deflation conditions with a slightly different unit, to pay back very much more than they actually borrowed.
Then the article goes on to say that Professor Fisher has recently issued a statement

Unemployment-Mr. Campbell
in which he gives it as his opinion that we are in for a period of low prices, business depression and unemployment. Professor Fisher states that the amount of gold that is being mined to-day is not sufficient to keep our currency up to the standard of our statutes, as far as maintaining the gold standard is concerned. He points out that the demands of commerce and industry for gold are very great; a large percentage of the gold mined is used in the filling of teeth and the making of jewellery, and there is not sufficient gold left to meet the requirements of our statutes in order to maintain a gold standard. Because of that fact, Professor Fisher points out that we are facing a period of low prices, of business stagnation, unemployment and distress.
Does that not seem an absurd situation? Let me put it in this way, to reduce the proposition to an absurdity. Supposing there were no gold mined at all; supposing all the gold mines in the world petered out and the production of gold ceased. Would that mean that if I have wheat to sell and some other man has clothing to sell, there is no medium of exchange by which he can buy my wheat and I can buy his clothes? That is exactly what it means, so long as we maintain this rather ridiculous system. Of course the gold standard is something like the British constitution, a thing which does not exist; because as a matter of fact we never have maintained the gold standard; there is not gold behind our currency as there is supposed to be. Our statutes are fairly flexible, and that is the only reason the system is workable at all. However, it does seem time that we began to inquire into this matter in order to try to get a permanent unit, something that would not be varying from day to day and causing all these business disturbances.
In a general way the unemployment problem is a result of the increased efficiency of the machines. There is no doubt about that, and that again is something governments cannot control and would not control even if they could. Let me again illustrate it in this way: Take the hypothetical case of say 1,000 people living on an island, with no contact with the outside world. We will say they have a perfect division of labour so that each person supplies his quota in the interests of the community. We will suppose that ten men have the responsibility of supplydng the community with food. If these men invent a machine which will reduce their hours of labour, or which will do the same work with two men instead of ten, would that mean there would be eight men doing nothing and being fed by the community? In a properly ordered com-

munity these extra hours of labour would be absorbed back into the whole community, and the hours of labour would be distributed all around and shorter periods of work would ensue. If they worked full time, some of the time previously expended could be used as extra time to produce luxuries and other unnecessary things. Of course, this is the idealistic way of considering this matter. We do not want to destroy the machine because an efficient machine is simply making a slave of the machine instead of the man; it is producing with less labour, but there is something wrong with our system when an efficient machine which does away with human labour is responsible for a great deal of unemployment, which in turn is responsible for misery and distress.
I believe that immigration has had a great deal to do with unemployment. I would like to read a report which appeared on February 28, in a Swift Current newspaper. This deals with the evidence given before the Saskatchewan royal commission on immigration, as follows:
J. S. Laycock, mayor of Swift Current, stated that in his opinion all immigration should be discontinued for a period of three to five years, or at any rate until the country had a chance to absorb and find employment for those already here. He was not opposed to immigrants coming to the country who had sufficient capital to establish themselves on the land and who would not become a charge on the province.
That gentleman went on to say that it would cost the town of Swift Current this year $5,000 for relief, and that is a very small town. He used some other pointed expressions regarding immigration. At the same sitting Mr. F. G. Westlake presented resolutions on behalf of the board of trade of Swift Current, which resolutions opposed immigration of any kind except in the case of those persons having sufficient capital to establish themselves and carry on without assistance. I cite these extracts as examples of the evidence presented before that commission. I would like to quote an editorial which appeared in the Manitoba Free Press on March 6, dealing with the recent immigration conference at Ottawa. That editorial refers to the statement made by the Prime Minister that unemployment was not a federal matter, but rather a matter which belonged to provincial and municipal governments. This editorial points out that recent immigration is a tremendous factor in unemployment. I quote:
For instance, Vancouver testified that 70 per cent of the men on its register were immigrants brought out here under some form of assisted immigration, and 58 per cent had been here less than five years.

Unemployment-Mr. Campbell
Calgary testified that 28 per cent of those unemployed were born out of Canada, and had come out to Canada during the past two years. The editorial refers to the fact that a very large proportion of the unemployed of Winnipeg were ex-service men, and it says:
Saskatoon declared that 40 per cent of the unemployed there were immigrants who should have gone on the land.
The editorial concludes:
-the general agreement seeming to be that 70 per cent of those on the list had been in Canada less than five years.
I realize that the government lately has changed its policy with regard to immigration. but even so I do not think the fact can be overemphasized that immigration has had a great deal to do with the unemployment problem, and I think this matter should be placed before the government for their future guidance.
Under the policy previously followed we have gone out into the highways and byways and pleaded with people and have done everything we could to induce thorn to come to this country. We have been doing our best to boiTOw the most terrible of all problems, the problem which confronts Europe and Asia, that of over-population. Canada should prize her free, open spaces, and should not be ready to give away the heritage of her people.
One of the causes of unemployment is the fact that the farmers are not purchasing as much as they did previously. One reason for this, although not the only one, is that agriculture has been made the shock absorber for the whole immigration policy. A deliberate attempt has been made, not only by the government, but by the transportation companies, to stimulate agriculture artificially, and when you artificially stimulate any industry or calling, whether it b<~ agriculture, manufacturing, or professional work, you throw the whole economic machine out of gear. Organized skilled labour has been able to hold a club over the head of the government, and it has been able to say: You must not bring in men to compete for our jobs. The unskilled labourer and the farmer are not so vocal, they are not so well organized; *consequently their industries have been forced to absorb the vast majority of the immigrants. I contend that the policy we have been following in the past is not only unjust and unfair, but it is unsound and uneconomic as a national policy. It would be just as fair and reasonable to advertise for *doctors, for lawyers, for school teachers, for manufacturers and such like to come in and lielp develop this country, as it is to bring in
farmers. I wonder what the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and his colleagues would say if we advertised in the newspapers of the United States and Great Britain in an effort to induce lawyers and professional men to come to this country and compete in their professions. There would be a terrible outcry from the members of those professions if anything like that were done. The farmer has not been so well organized, he has not been so vocal, and therefore his industry has been made the shock absorber.

speechtext: In that case we might get cheaper legal services.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HE.APS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Unemployment-Mr. Campbell
undertaken by any country in the history of the world. She proposes within the next few years to put under cultivation an additional
30,000,000 acres of land. Russia must produce an exportable surplus in order to pay for this machinery. That is a factor to be taken into account in the consideration of an immigration policy, and when we talk of breaking up more land and bringing more people into the country.
The new immigration policy recently announced by the minister is rather late. It seems to me it should have been put into effect many years ago. May I point out that to the extent to which we provide remedies to alleviate conditions in this country, to that extent will other people come in and try to absorb those remedies, and it may be necessary to provide an immigration policy that will protect our working people and farmers from too much outside competition. I have under my hand an article which appears in the last issue of the Financial Times. It is written by Mr. R. J. C. Stead, who, I understand, is publicity agent for the Department of Immigration. Mr. Stead points out that in 1900 Canada produced manufactured goods to the value of $481,000,000. In 1927 this figure had risen to $3,425,000,000, or an increase of 700 per cent. In spite of the fact, however, that the value of manufactured products increased by 700 per cent in the twenty-seven years, the number of employees in the factories increased by less than 100 per cent. He pointed out that Canadian agricultural products in 1901 were valued at $572,000,000. In 1927, only twenty-six years afterwards, this figure had risen to $2,224,000,000, or an increase of 400 per cent; but notwithstanding the large increase in the output, the rural population had in that time increased by only 33 per cent. He pointed out what I have already mentioned, that while there are complaints-and he was answering some of them -that the government was not bringing in a sufficient number of immigrants, never at any previous time in the history of the United States had that country been called upon to absorb so many immigrants in proportion to their own population. Mr. Stead further pointed out that since 1920 there was an increase of 22,388,000,000 tons of freight handled by United States railways. That is an enormous increase in the short period of nine years, but he pointed out that in spite of that huge increase there had been an actual reduction of 366,000 in the number of workers employed in that period.
My point is that Canada is capable, with the new and more efficient machinery we have, of making tremendous progress to-day

with her own natural increase in population. Of course I am not advocating the shutting of the door. As regards those who have the money to establish themselves and who wish to come in of their own volition, I have no objection to seeing them come in, but we should stop now, henceforth and forever all efforts by advertising and special inducement to bring people into this countiy. The trouble with the policy that we have been carrying on in the past is that it did not take into consideration the social and economic welfare of the people who were already here. Any immigration policy, present or proposed, should have as its only object the welfare and happiness of the people now in Canada. I quote from a recent newspaper dispatch some observations made by Professor Ottewell of the University of Alberta before the Canadian Club in Montreal:
Speaking before the Canadian Club in Montreal. A. E. Ottewell, of the University of Alberta, warned the capitalist class of the results that will flow from power farming, and advised that immigration should be curtailed in order that the farmers who were driven from the soil might find employment. He also advocated that "schools, churches and all social institutions should be overhauled to meet the new requirements."
Another newspaper article, dated at Winnipeg, November 29, in part reads:
Prof. A. R. M. Lower of Wesley College, Winnipeg, in a recent public lecture declared:
"We have no need of immigration to increase our population, and if immigrants in large numbers continue to come to us there can be but one result. Our own people-those who are born in this country-will have to go away. The presence or absence of immigration will not affect in the slightest degree the rate at which this country will grow."
"For sixty years," Prof. Lower proceeded, "we in Canada have been receiving so many immigrants that we have had to embark a large proportion of native-born for the United States. This proves that, in five years out of six we have had more than sufficient man power.
" 'Cheap' men will always drive out 'dear' men. The man who is willing to take the least stays here; the other goes away.	About
1,000,000 persons, native-born and immigrants, have left this country for the United States in the last seven years. This simply turns us into a training ground for United States citizens. The advent of the immigrant lowers the standard of living and makes the opportunities to the south of us loom larger in the eyes of the native-born.
"Artificial accession by way of immigration is at least only so much waste effort-at worst, a form of racial suicide."
May I refer hon. members to a very interesting book called Mankind at the Crossroads, written by Professor East of Harvard university? Professor East lays down the

Unemployment-Mr. Campbell
doctrine that population tends to increase with available food and land supplies and opportunities existing within the country. His doctrine conflicts rather with that we call the Malthusian theory, that put forward by Professor Malthus of Oxford. In this connection may I quote some figures from his book? Professor East gives the rate of increase per thousand of population in the various outstanding countries of the world, and he also gives at the present rate of increase the number of years it will take the respective countries to double their population. The figures are as follows:
