Canada, because of its opportunities, increases the most rapidly in population. Professor East states that if Canada can support
60,000,000 people she will do well, and he says that she will approach that number in less than three-quarters of a century. The crux of Professor East's argument is that immigration does not and cannot increase the population; that to the extent to which we bring people in and absorb them in this country, to that extent we either drive our own people out or prevent their natural increase. That is a very interesting theory, and it is well worth considering.
The Prime Minister in his speech seemed to fear the demands on the treasury which would result from any federal measure of unemployment relief, and objected to taxing the people to assist the provinces to that end. He stated that hiis government, the Liberal government, was elected on a pllatform of economy, and he objected to taking money out of the federal treasury for the purpose of relieving unemployment. I have just the same objection as the Prime Minister has to taking money out of the treasury, but if he examines the public aocounts he will realize he will save enough money for this purpose if he will practise economy in other things. If economy is the policy on which his government was elected; if that is the policy of the Liberal government, I would suggest that he practise it a little. Take for instance the expenditures on the Governor General s office, Rideau Hall and so forth: this year it cost nearly $441,000 and since the present government took office there has been a steady increase. Surely we could cut that in two and save a quarter of a million dollars. These figures are not final, because we spend on vice-regal oars a great deal of money which is charged up to the Canadian National Railways and which does not show in the public accounts. Last year we spent $149,000 on the citadel at Quebec. This has been discussed here so often that I do not wish to weary the house with it now, but the figures are startling. Their Excellencies, I understand, spend only about two or three weeks in the summer at the citadel, and yet we find this enormous expenditure of money. Let me give one or two items in the list of expenditures for the Quebec citadel, taken from the Auditor General's report for 1908-29:
Carpet, 1,8719 yards	 $10,036.09
(Purchased from the Brinton-Peterborough Carpet Company, Peterborough.)
There is also an item for renovating and plastering the ballroom, at a cost of $7,712. It seems to me that when women and children are suffering because of unemployment in this country, we could very well do without these expenditures. The ballroom, I suppose, would be used only two or three times in twelve months. If the Prime Minister would go over these expenditures, he would easily find where he could save money enough to relieve unemployment without dipping into the treasury.
Take the expenditure on automobiles for the government, which was mentioned by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie). That expenditure has 'been increasing steadily year after year, and the Auditor General year after year has been complaining about it. May I read a note, under the heading of automobiles and operating costs, in the introduction to the public accounts of 1928-29. The Auditor General states:
The total expenditure in connection with new automobiles and automobile repairs, renewals, etc., but not including cost of gasoline and lubricants, amounted to $634,549.10, an increase of $92,622.46. or 17 per cent over the expenditure of 1927-28.
The Auditor General goes on to comment on that increased expenditure and to plead for a reduction. He made the same sort of comment in the public accounts of last year. He complained of a similar increase over the

Unemployment-Mr. Brady
year before. I commend that to the consideration of the Prime Minister as a means of saving money to provide for the relief of the needy unemployed without increasing taxation at all. Undeniably there is unemployment in the cities and destitution on many of our farms. As a matter of fact, in western Canada to-day the land is rapidly passing out of the hands of those who toil on it. I do not know about the eastern provinces, but in western Canada landlordism and tenantry is almost as bad as it is in Europe. Those are conditions that we dislike to mention, but there they are, staring us in the face, and there is no use running away from them.
I agree with what was said by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) as to the effect of poverty itself. Some people are accused of a lack of thrift, but their condition more often than not is the effect of poverty rather than the cause of it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HE.APS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise with very much pleasure to support the amendment of the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) and his plea that immediate action be taken by the government in regard to unemployment.
Unemployment is not confined to Canada. It is a problem w'hich we must all acknowledge belongs to every country in the world, and it is receiving the attention of statesmen everywhere and of legislatures the world over. In Canada we see, on the one hand, every mark of prosperity and wealth; we see millions of dollars passing in and out of the country for imports and exports; we see our trade and commerce expanding; we see thousands of our citizens living in security and sometimes in the lap of luxury; but, on the other hand, standing idle in Canada to-day are hundreds of thousands of our fellow citizens, the very rank and file who are producing the wealth from which the nation benefits. They are physically able and willing to work, but the opportunity for work is not there. Others of our citizens, though at present engaged in work, have at all times the dread of unemployment hanging over their heads like the sword of Damocles. These, Mr. Speaker, are just the simple facts. The fear of unemployment is the most tragic and appalling problem that besets the great mass of men and women to-day. It is the paramount evil in the workman's life. His livelihood, his savings, his family, everything that is dear to him, is very often threatened by unemployment. His one great fear is that he will be out of work. The right to work, the right to get a fair wage for work, the right to earn 
the necessities of life, is the privilege of every man. It is based both upon divine and civil law. The causes of unemployment the world over are so numerous and varied that it would be impossible for me to enumerate them. I shall therefore attempt to speak only of the causes of unemployment in Canada itself as I see them, and before I conclude I shall offer what I believe to be the solution of this problem, or one that will at least reduce unemployment to the minimum in Canada.
We have the common accidents of life. We have sickness. We have casual and seasonal unemployment. We have the irregularity of large public works being carried on at intervals by the provinces and by the federal government. We have the closing down of industrial plants. We have new industrial methods developed in the interests of efficiency to increase output, with a consequent decrease in the number of workmen employed. We have likewise within Canada to-day the slow but steady destruction of our primary and sometimes of our secondary industries. We see this country being flooded by manufactured goods in an enormous volume, the great majority of which could be manufactured here. We are sending out millions of dollars-nine hundred million dollars went to the United States last year-for manufactured goods. Seventy per cent of this could be kept within Canada to build up our industries. I am simply stating facts as I know them. Unemployment, greater or less, must always be found as the natural corollary of our modern industrial system. Never can unemployment be eliminated; it is a by-product, it is the very shadow of our modern industrial life. But by a study of the causes of unemployment in any given locality, in any given province, or throughout the whole Dominion, and by the cooperation of the employer and employee, the provincial and the federal governments, ways and means can be found to reduce this unemployment to a minimum.
To make my position clear on this matter,
I wish to say, Mr. Speaker, that I firmly believe it is a sacred duty, incumbent upon this parliament, sedulously to watch for and provide ways and means to cope with the unemployment problem which is increasing in this country to-day to such an- alarming extent. In the middle ages, labour was mostly agricultural and held in bondage by the feudal lords, but in the towns and cities it was controlled by the guilds. Later the state took control and began to interest itself in labour. You will recall that in England the Statute of Labourers was enacted which restrained workmen from wandering around the country, and likewise set the rate of wages,

Unemployment-Mr. Brady
and these wages they were obliged to accept. But with the rise and development of modern industry the whole aspect of labour changed, with the result that the character of the relationship changed, and it has been recognized by every commisison that has investigated labour conditions that the obligation to reduce unemployment rests, not upon a municipality, not upon any particular division of the commonwealth, but upon the commonwealth as a whole. In other words, unemployment is a national reseponsibility. Yesterday the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) endeavoured to limit the significance of the word "national", just as later he also endeavoured to limit the significance of the word "state," to a province merely. I do not accept the limitation, Mr. Speaker, and I feel there are many reasons why this parliament should take part in reducing unemployment throughout the whole dominion. In proportion as the state receives wealth from labour and from industry in the form of income and other taxes, and as the federal Minister of Labour is concerned with labour throughout all the provinces, it is but right that this parliament should take appropriate action so that every man who is physically fit and willing to work should be given at least a fair chance of obtaining employment at good wages.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to get before the house what I believe is recognized by the great masses of the people to-day to be fundamental. Our present government-I want to get that home-our present government is responsible for something that is not only a tragedy, it is a shameful blot upon our fair Dominion. In what way, I am asked. I reply, many of Canada's sons and daughters are leaving the country, as every hon. member knows, simply because they cannot get employment within her boundaries. And sir, for the last two days we have been trying to shift the responsibility for unemployment and throw it to the four winds of heaven for the league of nations or some other body to take up. I was surprised when I heard the argument advanced that unemployment was a matter that did not concern this parliament. England is a thousand years old, and is it any wonder that she should have unemployment; is it any wonder that after those many years with her intensive industrial life that unemployment prevails there? But when you come to Canada, a young country of great natural resources, to which the eyes of Britain are looking in the hope that Canada will assist in solving some of her problems, what do we find? We find that Canada herself is unable to cope with this problem of unemployment. I
think we should bow down our heads in shame to be paraded before the empire and before the world at this hour as a country unable to cope with it. Is it not humiliating to reflect that with our small population and our great natural resources we cannot give to our ablebodied, physically fit men the right which is theirs to do a day's work and so get an assurance that at least they will be able to provide their wives and children with the necessaries of life?
I have heard yet no argument advanced by the Prime Minister, nor by the Minister of Labour, nor by any other hon. gentleman that would cause me to change my view that unemployment is a national problem, that is, a problem for the federal authorities to deal with. In their efforts to shift the responsibility to the provinces the municipalities they have moved around in a large circle, but on no occasion have they come out and declared the faith that is in them. I honour a noble opponent, I respect the man who differs from me politically, but I want to know exactly the basis of his political faith. During the past year while crossing Canada I have watched deputations of the unemployed and on the city streets I have noted the crowds waiting patiently for work, and the sorry state of affairs has always brought to my mind a countryman of mine, Oliver Goldsmith, who at a period when something similar was happening to his country, wrote these lines:
111 fares the land, to hastening ills a prey,
Where wealth accumulates, and men decay:
Princes and lords may flourish, or may fade;
A breath can make them, as a breath has made;
But a bold peasantry, their country's pride,
When once destroyed, can never be supplied.
More governments have been defeated by failing properly to estimate public opinion upon vital questions concerning the wellbeing, happiness and material success of the people than from any other cause. I wish to say to-night that such a question is before the people of Canada, one which concerns their well-being, their material success and their happines. I may recall to the house an occasion somewhat similar to this in 1910 when Sir Wilfrid Laurier, doubting the advice of his friends, decided to go west and learn the state of public opinion in those western provinces. Therefore, in the months of July and August he crossed western Canada. Here was a popular man, one who had won the respect of all, welcomed by foe as well as by friend through the years of his political life. What did he find? He found that instead of admiration he was received with cold criticism; in place of applause he received silence, and

Unemployment-Mr. Brady
the result was that before the election of 1911 came he anticipated exactly what was going to take place. He found at that time, as I believe the present government will find when it goes to the country, that the voice of public opinion was against the policy which his government was pursuing. Agriculture is the key industry of Canada; my friends opposite will no doubt admit that. Moreover, it is not merely a key industry; it is a vital factor in times of national defence; it is at all times the basis of material welfare of the people of Canada. That being the case, let us look at a few very important facts to illustrate what I said a moment ago. Agriculture, the great primary industry of Canada, has been strangled by the action of this government. Do you want proof to show where we are drifting in regard to this basic industry? If that is what you wish, I will quote figures. In the last ten years the animal products of Canadian farms have decreased from $156,000,000 down to $55,000,000. In 1920 Canada was an exporter of every principal animal product, but to-day our Dominion is an importer of bacon, butter, mutton and lamb. The export of other animal products at the present time is a mere fraction of the 1920 figure. An outstanding fact is, to my mind, that for the first time in forty years Canada's exports of bacon to Great Britain are nil; yet the United Kingdom imports annually over 900,000,000 pounds of that particular commodity.
Why pursue what we all know to be the case? It would not be in order for me to attempt to alter the viewpoint of those who persist in saying that the fiscal policy of a country plays no part in the solution of the unemployment problem. I wish to say that if we could keep within Canada 60 per cent of the $900,000,000 we paid out during the last year for manufactured goods imported from the United States we would not have an unemployment problem to-day, and we would not be faced with the amendment which is presented for our consideration. On that point I wish to say that as far as I can see, after reading the steps that have been taken in other countries in regard to social legislation and unemployment insurance, there is merit in the proposal. It draws to the attention of the government, the employer and everybody concerned, the importance of solidifying industry. Marine and fire insurance, when first introduced, did not have the expected results which were later realized, yet we find over two-thirds of the expected fires did not take place; the same may apply to unemployment insurance. If that be the case I see great merit in this particular insurance 
scheme. Yet we heard the Prime Minister put forth yesterday the argument which precluded the possibility of this parliament having anything to do with the relief of the unemployment problem.
Before I speak about the Prime Minister I would like to say a word to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan), and I shall try to speak in a way which, owing to his genial nature, he will understand. When he made the speech the other evening covering such a wide range of subjects, and to a great extent subjects which were very remote from the problem before him, I was reminded of an Irish story. An Irishman went to Australia, and while there he saw the Australian parakeet for the first time. It is a beautiful bird with golden plumage and variegated feathers. This particular bird was sitting in a tree, and the Irishman became so interested and absorbed in the beauty of the bird that he determined to catch it. As it was in the suburbs of the city he climbed the tree, and when about to put his hand on the bird he heard the remark, "Hello, what do you want?" The Irishman thereupon lifted his hat and said: "Oh, excuse me, sir, I thought you were a bird." Until the other evening I thought the Minister of Labour was the Minister of Labour, but now I would call him the Minister of laissez faire, because I think he very nicely went over a delicate problem and left it untouched.
Furthermore, coming to the speech of the Prime Minister, I think he did not realize the gravity of the situation as the people of Canada see it to-day. Before I go on with that point, I wish to draw attention to a state of unemployment which I know particularly well, and which exists in my own part of Canada. We have among the fishermen of British Columbia the finest and most daring body of men in the world. They are out on the stormy waters in the depths of winter, dashed and lashed by the infuriated gales, in quest of what? They are there in order to secure the rich products of the sea, bringing it into port in order that thousands of people in their luxurious and well looked after home3 can sit down and enjoy that food. What is this government doing for the fishermen on the Pacific coast? I will tell you, sir, that there is an immediate way to stop unemployment and to help Canadian men give a little more comfort to their wives and children, to which they are entitled. Why, sir, we always believed that beneath the British flag we found not merely justice and equity but consideration on the part of those who were in power. The fishermen of the coast, in their very own harbours, have to pay two cents a pound on halibut which is taken out m

Unemployment-Mr. Brady
bond and sent to the markets of the United States. Furthermore, they are being threatened with an extra 5 cents per pound on this frozen halibut. Right now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that if the Conservative party, to which I have the honour to belong, were in power it would not be more than twelve months before the men at present unemployed would be working, and in five years from now not merely would every man be employed but we could employ one million more of our own kith and kin. It is no use disguising the fact, sir, I will go further and say that under our present policy the government of this country, to use a simile understood by all, is taking the ship of state down a stream whose loud and resounding roar indicates that there are cataracts of danger ahead, not merely for Canada but for the empire as well. That is a statement the truth of which any man who wishes to examine matters will see for himself.
Now, sir, the next step is to turn to the Prime Minister's statement, and I wish to say that it astonished everyone. I see the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) would like a little story, so I shall tell him one. A gentleman was caught by his wife kissing the cook.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HE.APS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HE.APS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Is that unparliamentary? His wife said to him: "John, you surprise me." He had a little more knowledge of grammar and of correct speech than she, so he replied "No, my dear; you are astonished, but I am surprised." When the Prime Minister last evening made to this house and flung to the four winds of Heaven the terrific pronouncement that he would not give five cents to a province that had a government that was not Liberal, I was astonished, and I want to say that the very dykes that he has been standing behind, and which were supporting the Liberal party in Canada, were swept away by public opinion, and the flood waters of indignant public opinion were let loose over the Liberal party. I do not want to exaggerate, but I will tell you the effect produced by the words of the Prime Minister last evening. He stood representing the Liberal party, which is the supposed party of freedom for democracy, but no oligarch of Russia; not even Alexander of Macedonia, that savage king; not the tyrants of Syracuse; not even the Roman dictators ever held a bludgeon over the heads of their people equal to the threat made by the Prime Minister last evening. Why, sir, he delivered an ultimatum last night to Canada, and as he stood there I was reminded of days during the time of the ancient Roman empire,
when the plebeians of that time were whipped by officers and forced to cry out in the market place, "Non habemus regem, nisi Caesarem" in other words, "we shall have no king but Caesar." They were flogged to declare before the world that everything was all right with Rome. Last evening the people of six provinces that are not flaunting the flag of Liberalism were told to cry out, "we shall have no king but the Prime Minister, who sits in Ottawa to-day." That is exactly the message that he tried to inculcate; and now I see a little behind the scenes. Is it any wonder that in districts and constituencies that were not supporting the Prime Minister we found it most difficult to obtain from the Minister of Public Works the needed requirements which would help unemployment in those parts of Canada? This is an absolute corollary to the statement of the Prime Minister. He said last evening something so unusual in the annals of the great Liberal party, something so unusual in the annals of every great party of any country, that we must wipe out this insult if we are true to our principles and to that which we hold highest and dearest. That is, that no matter what party we belong to, the party of power will be impartial and will do what they feel they should do, whether or not the representatives of any part of Canada belong to that party. That is what our party would do, and furthermore I wish to say that if I could not believe that the Conservative party when they come into power would be able to bring back Canada to her righful place within the empire I would unhesitatingly sever my connection with that party. Should this government remain in power longer we shall have gone too far down the precipice and it will be difficult to retrace our steps and build up this country. This offers food for reflection. Unemployment is undoubtedly something which should concern us all; it should be paramount to every other consideration.
The great mass of the ten million people in this country, those who rear their families and give stalwart sons to Canada, are waiting to see what political party is able to build up this Dominion and take from our natural resources that which will enable them to live. What a pallid page is offered for the people of Canada to read in the record of the Liberal party during the last six years! It is a pallid, wane page of weak endeavour and of hopeless incapacity to realize the great possibilities open to them had they been true and faithful to their trust.
When our party returns to power, as I believe it will, it will be for the salvation of
Unemployment-Mr. Bird

Canada and the empire. I have no political bias, but I believe, as the majority of Canadians believe, that the future destiny of Canada, at least for some years to come, is linked and bound up with the Conservative party.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HE.APS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I always listen with great pleasure to the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Brady). If the force of his argument were equal to the charm of his Irish eloquence, it would be unnecessary for me to rise in my place, but I am afraid that something more needs to be said.
Representing as I do a constituency which is speedily becoming industrialized, I could not permit this opportunity to pass without giving my point of view. At the outset I iesire to say that I will endeavour to make my remarks as uncritical as possible, but I would like to use what persuasive powers I have to influence the government to change its attitude on this question. I think that what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) have said is true, that Canada, like most countries, needs to be educated regarding this question. I am afraid that the fact that we are not educated has had some bearing upon the attitude adopted by the government. It seems to me that a government should be a leader of public opinion as well as a follower. I have said already this session that governments tend to follow the line of least resistance, and I am afraid that the unemployed worker belongs to a class which is practically a political nonentity, an unorganized class, and one which has no means of bringing its political power to bear effectively upon this house. Possibly the unemployed themselves are to blame, but it seemed to me a very significant thing when I heard that Tom Moore, the leader of organized labour in this country, was not in favour of any move being taken along the lines of this amendment. Upon that fact I think there hangs a tale. The aristocrat of labour, like the government, has very little real feeling-

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HE.APS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I know the hon. member does not desire to say anything which may be in error. I do not know that Mr. Moore ever has said that or has been accused of saying it. The only reference to that question is the fact that the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada endorsed the action of the government in not calling a conference.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HE.APS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Still my point has force, that we have a class of workingmen in Canada which is not organized, a class which finds itself in the queue at the soup kitchen. These
	^
men are large in number, but they are not organized; they have no means of making their position felt in the house; they have no one to lobby for them in Ottawa.
The unorganized classes, whether they be farmers or labourers, must learn a lesson: that there is only one way in which they can get justice from the powers that be, namely, through organization. I see very little hope of the unemployed receiving consideration from any government until they become organized so that their diffused power may be focused. There is a good deal of inertia to be overcome among all classes in this country.
A few years ago a prominent public man in the United States said that if ever that country had a revolution it would be produced not by the bolsheviks but by the boneheads. The bonehead constitutes a very large class in any industrialized country, and that class is made up of many varieties. One variety is composed of people who are moved by crass stupidity in regard to social and economic matters. I have actually heard pious people quoting the Scriptures in order to prove that the solution of the unemployment problem was hopeless because the Author of Christianity once upon a time said that the poor will always be with us. That is one kind of attitude which still obtains in almost every industrialized country-a hopeless, stupid outlook upon this question. There is also what I would describe as the Pharisee in modern economic life, the man *who says: If a man is unemployed he has nobody to blame but himself; it is his own fault. Does anyone deny we have that class in Canada? You can find in every city and town the man who, with a superior air, says that if a man is unemployed it is his own fault. I remember years ago reading the life of Will Crooks, one of the first labour members at Westminster. That story of Will Crooks' life cured me of that attitude. He was a man representing the best type of British workman who in his young married life walked the streets of London day after day, and only by an extraordinary amount of will power saved himself from going over the precipice and becoming one of London's unemployables.
There are other attitudes which have been taken. There is the attitude taken by the Prime Minister the other day. I know the Prime Minister is not a stupid man; I would not classify him with people who are labouring under traditional views on this question, but just the same his speech was a real disappointment to me, a disappointment all the keener because some of us saw that speech on the background of the Prime Minister's

Unemployment-Mr. Bird
own mind, a mind that is illuminated with modern economic truth; and I say that a speech such as he delivered the other day was on that account all the more lurid in its deficiency. As I analysed the speech as he went along, I found he gave seven arguments against doing anything immediately for the unemployed in this country. Each of those arguments individually was to me very unconvincing. Collectively they lacked logical coherence; there was running through them no thread of reason. I have not time tonight to refer to them in detail and if I had it would possibly be superflous, because others have adequately dealt with them. Some of those arguments were very far-fetched. For instance the Prime Minister said that stressing unemployment conditions would act detrimentally upon the flow of capital to Canada. That is a far-fetched argument; it is an unworthy argument, because, after all, capital does not enter into the same category with suffering human beings. But from another standpoint, as someone said this evening, it is not right, it is not safe, to hide an evil. It is not safe to talk in quiet tones about something that , is festering in the body politic. When the Prime Minister said that, he reminded me of the refined old lady who died of gastric trouble. The reason she died was because she always told the doctor she had a pain in the chest; she was ashamed of saying where the pain really was. If we Canadians get into the habit of covering over, glozing over, the social evils that are corroding our national life, the possibilities are that those evils will presently become a focal point that will gradually poison our social life. A labouring class-and I dislike using that term-that is well taken care of, that is relieved of its fears, is in any country one of the things that will attract not only capital but everything else we desire to have as a country.
Some of the Prime Minister's arguments were, if not far-fetched, plausible. I am not going to enter into a discussion in regard to the British North America Act because I think that has been very well dealt with. But there was one argument that struck me as being altogether misplaced and it was this: the Prime Minister said:	If we yield to this
plea it will mean favouring one class of the community, namely, the labouring class, but the farming class and the professional class will be left out in the cold. I have only one way to answer that and it is this: that the attitude, the spirit, that is out to readjust industrial conditions in this country is the attitude, the spirit that will ultimately adjust
farming matters. Fundamentally the farmer and the industrial worker stand upon common ground. Any attempt to divide their interests can be successful only so long as those two classes do not understand wherein their interests lie. In fact, I cannot see any hope for either the farmer or the industrial worker until they understand the common ground upon which they stand. The spirit in which we in this comer are supporting the industrial worker is identical with the spirit in which we support the producer. After all, it is the attitude, the spirit, which counts.
As to responsibility, the Prime Minister, while recognizing the problem, tried to escape the responsibility. As I view the matter, as I have heard the causes of unemployment discussed in this debate, every cause of the condition we have been referring to points to the national parliament. The problem is a national one, in the only sense in which the word "national" can apply. I am not going to enumerate to-night the causes of unemployment because I would be merely going over ground that has already been traversed; but each cause that has been discussed during this debate resolves itself into a question of policy that belongs to the federal parliament. I do not know of any single cause of unemployment that belongs to any particular section. Take it, for instance, from the point of view of the Conservatives to our right. They say that unemployment is due to the policy of low tariffs that is formulated in this house. It seems to me that a Conservative government when in power would, by the very force of its own position, have to formulate a policy for unemployment. They recognize the unemployment problem as originating here. But the same logic applies to my friends the Liberals. However much they try to shirk the inference, we know that the enactment of a fiscal policy either one way or the other will displace labour in this country; there is no question about that. This house wields an instrument which is potent for good or ill to the labouring men. If you raise the tariff, you certainly put men out of work. If you lower the tariff, you certainly put men out of work.

speechtext: Why?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HE.APS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That question has been answered so frequently that I would have thought my hon. friend's education would have been, by this time, well advanced along that line. We cannot escape the logic of the situation. My hon. friend says that he represents labour in this house, and I accord to
Unemployment-Mr. Bird

him the honour which he claims for himself. Let me read the pronouncement of one of the most outstanding labour men at the present time. In my opinion he is one of the most sincere labour men in Great Britain, a man who has suffered a great deal for his principles. I refer to Hon. Mr. Lansbury. In regard to this very question that my hon. friend has interjected he saj's, speaking of the Labour government of which he is a member:
We also tackled the question of free trade and tariff reform, taking our stand that neither of these shibboleths could ever be a solution of the poverty problem. We pointed out that in this land, under free trade and free competition, women, children, even babies were exploited; that slums and workhouses, mental asylums, and all social disorders of our day were the accompaniments both of protection and free trade. We also proved that the state and municipal socialist action was absolutely necessary to curb the terrible social evils which, during the days of free trade and protection had grown up in the great industrial centres owing to the reckless manner in which trade and industry were carried on. We argued that neither tariffs nor free trade do secure decent standards of life for our people.
I think that is a sufficient answer to my hon. friend, because while I accord to him the privilege which he claims of representing labour in Canada, yet at the same time I think the Hon. George Lansbury is an authority equal with his own. I was intending to come to that point a little later.
My purpose at the present time was not to enter into a controversy on the tariff. I was pointing out that the government wields an instrument that may at any moment displace labour in this country. I am not speaking of the eventualities that may happen years from now. Any serious change in fiscal policy almost at once displaces labour from one end of the country to the other, and if this parliament has any human feeling at all it would never presume to make any such change unless it provided for the displacement of labour that would surely be one of the fruits of its policy. We are coming to a time when the people are going to demand such humane consideration on the part of parliaments. They say to parliaments: We are not so much concerned with your policies as with their effects upon human beings. We want protection for human beings.
I want to conclude my remarks by stressing that point. I would like to appeal to the humanity of the Prime Minister. I do not think from what I know of him that an appeal like that will be altogether lost. I am not one who mocks at the idealism of the Prime Minister. I think that it is one of the finest manifestations that we have in CanatMr. Bird.]
dian public life. The fact that it may not have borne fruit is a matter for further discussion, but the fact that we have a Prime Minister who does show some comprehensive knowledge of these problems is, I think, something gained. It is a starting point at any rate; but, of course, it ought not to stop there. I would like to appeal to the Prime Minister's idealism. I know that other appeals are perhaps obscured by considerations of party, by presuppositions that really do not relate to the human element. But clearly this is a matter of human importance. Here is something that concerns the immediate well-being of men, women and children.
There are in the final analysis only two kinds of economic theory in existence; there have been only two ever since men have exchanged products with one another. The first theory was crystallized into a doctrine over a hundred years ago, a theory which postulated that the way to make a country great and wealthy was to subordinate the individual to the state, that the only way to build up a country in grandeur, in material possessions, was to forget the individual, to subordinate him to the necessities of the state. The other theory was the reverse. It maintained that the true economics was the economics which subordinated the state of the individual.

of political organization which when it attempts to make its appearance stultifies idealism. These conditions, however, cannot remain much longer. As far as the farmers of Canada are concerned I believe they are going to come forward with a type of political organization which will express their political aspirations more successfully than has been done in the past. It has not been done with much success in the past, I must admit, but it is only twenty-five years since the inception of the Labour party in England, and during that quarter of a century the Labour party, with its idealism and social ideals has fought with great success against entrenched privilege in England.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HE.APS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Wherein will the new
farmers' party differ from the other party?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HE.APS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I am not taking much stock in the new farmers' party. I do not think the solution lies in any particular type of party; I think we have had enough lessons to satisfy us that the attempt to start new and pure parties is doomed to failure. I do say this, however, that the economic organizations of the west, such as the pool organization in Manitoba, have enlisted 37,000 fanners to act in cooperation. We have never experienced a more complete organization in Manitoba than the one we have at the present time. There are 37.000 farmers organized around the ideal of cooperation. In my opinion the farmers of Manitoba can afford to forget about party politics, because they have formed an organization which has more political power than any political party the west will ever produce. I wonder what special privilege will throw the gauntlet down to the cooperating farmers of western Canada; I know of no power in Canada which has sufficient political influence to do it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HE.APS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have in my hand a clipping from the Toronto Globe of April 3, 1930. It is as follows:
No fewer than 188 homeless men were given shelter at the local gaol during March. This figure, according to police chief A. L. Church, is without precedent in the town's history.
This extract refers to the town of Orillia, and as that town is in my riding I would like to say that the men here referred to are not residents of Orillia. They are unfortunate men who are travelling from place to place in an attempt to find employment which is
[Mr. B.rd.l
denied them. Although guilty of no crime they are forced to spend their nights in gaol. I learned yesterday from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that even if the Dominion government were inclined to grant aid to the different provinces to help the unfortunate unemployed, these men would not receive any assistance. The reason is that they unfortunately live in the province of Ontario, a Conservative province and therefore subject to the exclusion mentioned by the Prime Minister. A man in Nova Scotia, Saskatchewan or New Brunswick would be in a similar plight. However, if a person similarly situated had the good fortune to live in the province of Quebec or Prince Edward Island but was unfortunate enough to be unemployed, he would receive such aid as might be afforded by this government. When have the free men of Ontario, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and other Conservative provinces lost the right to elect men of their own choice? Since when has the Prime Minister of Canada become so autocratic that he can arbitrarily dictate which provinces shall receive government aid for unemployed, and which provinces shall be refused that aid? Are the citizens of Ontario, the chief contributors to the public funds, to be denied the rights accorded to citizens of other provinces? May I suggest to the Prime Minister that as a public man, no matter how bitter his private views may be with respect to those politically opposed, he should remember the well known motto of " equal rights to all and special privileges to none."
I take it that one of the first duties of a government is to make such provision that work may be available to citizens of the country whose affairs it administers; that the men who live in that country may have employment and thus be enabled to maintain their homes and support their families. A nation cannot exist without people; people cannot exist without homes; homes cannot be maintained without money, and money can be obtained only by work. I have taken the trouble to look through the speech from the throne delivered at the begining of this session and placed before this house for its consideration, and I look in vain for a proposal which would hold out any hope for the unfortunate unemployed. Such proposals are always welcome, but they would be doubly welcome at this time of unemployment, stress and strain.
I look back upon the record of this government and I find that in many instances it has failed to live up to its responsibilities to the people. The Minister of Labour (Mr. APRIL 4, 1930
Unemployment-Mr. Thompson
Heenan) in his speech the other evening said that this government was having a ferry boat built in Canada in order to give work to Canadians. He told us that the government could have had this boat built more cheaply in England than in Canada. I am glad that the government is awakening to the fact that the people expect that every boat which is constructed to carry on the trade and commerce of this country and is the property of the Dominion government shall be built in this country, in Canadian shipyards, by Canadian workmen and with Canadian materials. The pity of it is that this government has been so slow to realize its duty in this regard. Within the past two or three years the government has had constructed abroad, instead of being built in Canada, a fleet of boats for use in the West Indies service. I have here the names of the boats with the cost of construction, as follows:
Lady Somers	 $1,737,138
Lady Rodney	 1,741,534
Lady Nelson	 1,541,230
Lady Hawkins	 1,544,757
Lady Drake	 1,548,101
That is a total of $8,112,762 which went out of the country, we have the boats, but they have our money. Had a proper patriotic Canadian policy been pursued, these boats would have been built in our own country; we would have the boats, and the money would have been circulated among our own people, giving employment to Canadian labourers and mechanics and providing a market for our merchants as well as for farm products. Some one may say, "Well, the boats would have cost more had they been built in Canada." That is possible, but as far as I am concerned I am in favour of a policy of having all government-owned vessels built in Canada, and in the case of these particular boats I understand that they could have been built in this country for practically the same money.

speechtext:
I think it is only fair to inform my hon. friend that tenders were 2419-S3i
called for from both British and Canadian shipyards. If I recall correctly, the cost of building these ships in Canada would have been about 40 per cent more than the cost of building them in British yards. The argument used by Canadian National Steamships, who were to operate the ships and who own them, was that the cost of operating the boats at that much of an increase in the cost of construction would involve a heavy toll in respect to rates, and would bring about a national loss. My hon. friend is quite correct in saying that it is advisable to build in Canada, but at that time Canadian National Steamships thought the load would be too heavy.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT OF MR. HE.APS TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I still stand by my position. Even if these boats had cost more they should have been built in Canada, because the additional money would have been kept in this country and distributed among our own people. We would have given employment to our own workingmen, and that is what the people of Canada want.
How are our Canadian shipyards to be kept in an efficient state if the work which they can reasonably expect to get is sent abroad? There is the matter of repairs to vessels. I understand that a Canadian boat can go into an American port and have necessary repairs done, and when she returns to Canada she pays a duty of 25 per cent on the value of the repairs. On the other hand, if an American boat enters a Canadian port and has certain repairs done, when she returns to the American side she has to pay a duty of 50 per cent on the value of those repairs. Why cannot we have a government that will protect the Canadian workmen to the same extent that the American government protects the American labourer? The psople of this country have spent an enormous amount of money in the construction of canals and other aids to navigation, and it is reasonable to expect that wherever possible the Canadian people should get something in return through the construction of ships and repairs to ships in Canada. I am told that in the United States a vessel cannot enter the coastwise trade unless she has been actually built, registered and documented there, but we know that many of our private owners, following the example of this government, have gone across the line and bought ships in that country, bringing them back to enter the trade here in competition with our own boats manufactured in Canada.
130S

Unemployment-Mr. Thompson
Now, Mr. Speaker, contrast the building of these boats abroad with the policy which was pursued by the Conservative government when ships were built for the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. I understand these boats were practically all built in this country. They cost a lot of money; I believe the total was about $75,000,000, but out of that total $45,000,000 was spent in wages to Canadian workmen from Vancouver to Halifax, while $30,000,000 was spent for the purchase of Canadian material. Employment was given to our own shipyards, and the money was kept in this country. Everybody prospered by it; the labourer, the mechanic, the merchant, the farmer, all profited by this work being done in this country. That is a contrast between the policies pursued by the two different parties. Millions of dollars have been spent abroad in the construction of government-owned ships. In 1929, $31,000,000 was spent on agricultural implements imported from the United States, almost all of which could have been manufactured in this country. Is .that the way to help the unemployment situation here? Every day of the year we send out of Canada $2,500,000, chiefly to purchase American manufactured goods that could be made in this country. Is that the way to help the Canadian workman who has a home to maintain and children to clothe and feed? The closing of our woollen mills as a result of the tariff policy of this government threw out of employment men and women who had worked at that business, and also deprived the farmer of a market for his wool. Is that the way to help the unemployment situation? Why cannot we have more buying at home of Canadian manufactured goods? Imagine sending yearfy to the United States for manufactured goods $89 for every man, woman and child in Canada ! Why not take more pride in our own products; why not more loyalty to the goods manufactured in this country? I can well understand, Mr. Speaker, why there should be unemployment in over-populated countries whose natural resources have been depleted and exhausted, but in this young country of Canada, with its under-population and magnificent natural resources, there is no excuse or reason for that condition existing. If we had a proper fiscal policy, a proper national policy -Canada for the Canadians-unemployment would rapidly disappear and prosperity would return. The people of Canada shortly will be given an opportunity to settle this question, and all signs indicate that they are now realizing their responsibilities. When given that 
opportunity the people will speak in no uncertain terms, and a new era of prosperity will be ushered in with the advent of a new government. That famous declaration of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) that the death knell of protection had been sounded is going to sound the death knell of the present government.
